title: Amarillo rambutan (yellow rambutan): Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaTitle: Amarillo rambutan: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaDescription: Amarillo rambutan is a rambutan variety from Ponciano Batugal. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: Amarillo is a registered rambutan variety, also sold or known as yellow rambutan or NSIC Rm 05. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council in 2003 as NSIC 2003 Rm 05. Ponciano Batugal bred it. Its record notes a yield of 50 to 60 kg.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil, the kind of farm where Amarillo rambutan is grown

blocks.text: If you came here looking for yellow rambutan or NSIC Rm 05, this is the same rambutan. Its seller and farm sources add notes, listed at the end. Compare it with the others in our [rambutan variety finder](/crop-varieties/rambutan), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for fruit trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: **Yield:** a recorded yield of 50 to 60 kg.

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. The mother tree of Amarillo was about 10 years old and about 8 meters tall when it was registered. Its record notes a yield of 50 to 60 kg. It bears every year, with fruit in July September. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
No pest or disease ratings are published for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.

The pests and diseases that hit rambutan fields most often: [cacao pod borer](/pests/cacao-pod-borer), [anthracnose](/diseases/anthracnose), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

A fruit of Amarillo weighs about 34.12 grams, and its shape is oblong. The flesh is white and smooth. Its sweetness measured 22.35 degrees Brix, the share of sugar in the juice. Most table fruit tastes sweet from about 12 Brix up. The edible part is 60.67 percent of the fruit. Its fruiting season is July September, bearing annual.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Oblong, about 34 g, yellow skin, smooth, juicy white flesh, about 22 Brix, about 61 percent edible.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: the yellow skinned rambutan in the registry, with the highest edible share (about 61 percent). Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant Amarillo rambutan

Pick a registered selection whose flesh comes off the seed cleanly, which buyers pay more for. Plant budded trees. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is yellow rambutan the same as Amarillo?
items.a: Yes. yellow rambutan is another name for Amarillo, registered as NSIC 2003 Rm 05. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.
The record shows a recorded yield of 50 to 60 kg. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of Amarillo?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
